```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
```

This document is the R counterpart of the Python notebook
[Part 08 - LLMs as Research Assistants](../../Notebooks/Part%2008%20-%20LLMs%20as%20Research%20Assistants/Part%2008%20-%20LLMs%20as%20Research%20Assistants.ipynb).
Content analysis at scale used to require teams of trained coders; large
language models now offer to do the labeling for pennies. Whether their
labels are *defensible as research measures* is an empirical question
that this part answers the traditional way: a codebook, a gold-standard
sample, agreement metrics, and an honest baseline.

### Learning objectives

* Explain why automated annotation (LLM or otherwise) must be validated
  against human-coded gold labels before its output is used as a
  research measure.
* Read a codebook with category definitions and decision rules that
  both humans and an LLM can apply.
* Build an LLM annotation prompt with structured (JSON) output, and
  parse the responses defensively.
* Estimate the cost of an annotation job before running it.
* Compute and interpret accuracy, Cohen's kappa, confusion matrices,
  and per-category precision and recall, and explain why chance
  correction matters when categories are imbalanced.
* Read the disagreements, because that is where the methodology lives.

## Setup

```{r libraries}
library(bskyr)
library(tidyverse)
library(jsonlite)
library(lubridate)
```

Most of this document does **not** need Bluesky credentials. Only
Section 1, which collects a fresh corpus, calls the Bluesky API. The
codebook, the gold-standard labels, the keyword baseline, and the whole
validation run from files committed with the repository, so those
chunks are marked `eval=TRUE` and run for every reader. (The LLM call in
Section 4 needs an Anthropic API key instead, and explains itself
without one.)

As in every part of this series, the shared helper `bsky_client.R` looks
for credentials (an `atproto.json` file or bskyr's environment
variables), authenticates if it finds them, and sets `bsky_authed`. The
`knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = bsky_authed)` line then makes that flag the
default for the document: with credentials every chunk runs; without
them the document still knits, the Bluesky API chunks are skipped, and
the chunks marked `eval=TRUE` run regardless.

```{r connect}
source("bsky_client.R")
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = bsky_authed)
```

## 1. Collecting a corpus of posts

One account's original, non-reply posts — short, varied, and exactly the
kind of material a topic codebook is built for — collected with
[`bs_get_author_feed()`](https://christophertkenny.com/bskyr/reference/bs_get_author_feed.html). Two helpers from
`bsky_client.R` do the filtering: `is_repost()` flags posts the account
reposted from someone else, and `is_reply()` flags replies — including
replies whose parent post has since been deleted, which a check on the
parent alone would miss:

```{r corpus}
ACTOR <- "nytimes.com"

feed <- bs_get_author_feed(ACTOR, limit = 200)

posts <- feed |>
  filter(!is_repost(feed), !is_reply(feed)) |>   # helpers from bsky_client.R
  transmute(
    uri,
    created_at = map_chr(record, "created_at", .default = NA),
    text = map_chr(record, "text", .default = ""),
    like_count, repost_count, reply_count
  ) |>
  filter(str_squish(text) != "") |>
  slice_head(n = 150)

dir.create("data", showWarnings = FALSE)
write_csv(posts, "data/posts.csv")
write_json(
  list(actor = ACTOR, endpoint = "app.bsky.feed.getAuthorFeed",
       reposts_excluded = TRUE, replies_excluded = TRUE,
       n_collected = nrow(posts),
       collected_at = format(now("UTC"), "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ")),
  "data/collection_metadata.json", pretty = TRUE, auto_unbox = TRUE)

nrow(posts)
```

## 2. Constructing a codebook

A codebook is the *measurement instrument*: mutually exclusive,
collectively exhaustive categories with decision rules a stranger could
apply. We read through the account's posts before writing it — always
look at your data first. A news organization's feed mixes hard news
(elections, courts, war and diplomacy, immigration), a smaller stream of
science, health, and technology stories, and a large share of
everything else: sports from The Athletic, recipes, games, shopping
advice, and promotions for podcasts and newsletters. That suggests three
labels:

| Label | Definition |
|---|---|
| `politics` | Government, elections, campaigns, parties, politicians in office or running, courts and law enforcement as institutions, legislation, public policy (including immigration), the military, war, diplomacy, and political protest. |
| `science_tech` | Scientific research and findings, medicine and health science, regulatory decisions about scientific or technical substance, artificial intelligence, consumer technology, and the technology industry. |
| `other` | Everything else: crime, accidents, and disasters reported as events; sports; entertainment; food; lifestyle and service pieces; games; and the publisher's promotions. |

**Decision rules** resolve the predictable conflicts. The two that do
the most work on a news feed: **rule 2**, a sports or entertainment
setting doesn't decide the label — a World Cup referee denied a U.S.
visa is an immigration story (`politics`), while a ranking of World Cup
kits is `other`; and **rule 3**, crime and disasters are `other` unless
the post is about policy, a government response, or political
mobilization.

The codebook lives in one JSON file that the Python notebook reads too,
so both implementations apply *exactly* the same instrument. We read it
from the Python series' directory, as Part 05 reads its shared archive.
`read_json(simplifyVector = TRUE)` turns the file's lists into R
vectors; the codebook text is stored one line per element, so
`paste(collapse = "\n")` rebuilds it:

```{r codebook, eval=TRUE}
CODEBOOK_PATH <- file.path("..", "..", "Notebooks",
                           "Part 08 - LLMs as Research Assistants", "data",
                           "codebook.json")
codebook_data <- read_json(CODEBOOK_PATH, simplifyVector = TRUE)

CODEBOOK_VERSION <- codebook_data$version
LABELS <- codebook_data$labels
DEFAULT_LABEL <- codebook_data$default_label
CODEBOOK <- paste0(paste(codebook_data$codebook, collapse = "\n"), "\n")
KEYWORD_RULES <- codebook_data$keyword_rules   # a named list, one vector per label

cat("Codebook version:", CODEBOOK_VERSION, "\n\n")
cat(CODEBOOK)
```

## 3. Gold-standard labels

Validation requires labels we trust: humans read a sample and apply the
codebook. The Python series hand-coded 60 posts from this account and
committed them, and because they live in a plain CSV, the R series
validates against the *same* gold standard — a nice illustration of why
archives beat live collections for reproducibility.

> **An honesty note.** These are *example* labels coded by the tutorial
> authors so the validation runs end to end. Real research uses two or
> more trained coders working independently, reports their inter-coder
> reliability, and documents how disagreements were resolved before
> treating their consensus as gold.

```{r gold, eval=TRUE}
gold <- read_csv(
  file.path("..", "..", "Notebooks",
            "Part 08 - LLMs as Research Assistants", "data",
            "gold_labels.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
) |>
  mutate(label_rationale = replace_na(label_rationale, ""))

cat(nrow(gold), "gold-labeled posts,", sum(gold$label_rationale != ""),
    "with a written rationale\n")
count(gold, gold_label)
```

The bar chart makes the **imbalance** visible: `politics` and `other`
split most of the sample, and `science_tech` has only a handful of
posts. That *prevalence* will matter when we interpret agreement: with
so few `science_tech` posts, a single miss moves its recall a long way.
`factor(levels = LABELS)` keeps the bars in codebook order rather than
alphabetical order:

```{r gold-plot, eval=TRUE, fig.width=6, fig.height=3.5}
gold |>
  count(gold_label) |>
  mutate(gold_label = factor(gold_label, levels = LABELS)) |>
  ggplot(aes(gold_label, n, fill = gold_label)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(politics = "#4c72b0", science_tech = "#55a868",
                               other = "#c44e52")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Posts",
       title = paste0("Gold-label distribution (n = ", nrow(gold), ")")) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The rationales record *why* the decision rules produced each label. Each
one should cite a rule the codebook actually states — when these labels
were first coded, several applied judgments ("sports setting, but U.S.
immigration → politics") that the codebook never wrote down, which an
LLM reading the codebook could not have known. Rules 2–6 now state them:

```{r gold-rationales, eval=TRUE}
gold |>
  filter(label_rationale != "") |>
  transmute(text = str_trunc(text, 90), gold_label, label_rationale) |>
  head(4)
```

How many of the gold posts are still in today's live corpus? Posts get
deleted, which is why a gold standard records the text it coded. This
chunk needs the corpus from Section 1, so it checks with `exists()`
first and explains itself when there is none:

```{r gold-overlap, eval=TRUE}
if (exists("posts")) {
  cat(sum(gold$uri %in% posts$uri), "of", nrow(gold),
      "gold posts are in today's live corpus\n")
} else {
  cat("No live corpus collected (Section 1 needs Bluesky credentials);",
      "the validation below runs from the committed gold file.\n")
}
```

## 4. LLM annotation with the Claude API

### 4.1 The prompt

The prompt wraps the codebook and one post in XML-style tags and
demands strict JSON — a label and a confidence between 0 and 1. It is
character-for-character the prompt the Python notebook builds, so the
two implementations would send the model identical requests:

```{r prompt, eval=TRUE}
build_prompt <- function(codebook, post_text) {
  paste0(
    "You are a careful content-analysis research assistant. Apply the ",
    "codebook below to the post and respond with ONLY a JSON object — ",
    "no preamble, no markdown fences.\n\n",
    "<codebook>\n", codebook, "\n</codebook>\n\n",
    "<post>\n", post_text, "\n</post>\n\n",
    "Respond with exactly this JSON shape:\n",
    '{"label": "politics" | "science_tech" | "other", ',
    '"confidence": <number between 0 and 1>}'
  )
}

cat(str_trunc(build_prompt(CODEBOOK, gold$text[[1]]), 900))
```

### 4.2 The annotation loop

The Claude API is an ordinary HTTP API, so
[httr2](https://httr2.r-lib.org/) talks to it directly: build a request
with the authentication headers, attach the JSON body, perform it, and
parse the JSON response. Four robustness pieces surround the call:

* `httr2::req_retry()` retries a request that fails with a rate limit
  (HTTP 429) or a temporary server error, waiting longer each time.
* `tryCatch()` around each post means one failed request becomes one
  missing label, rather than an error that discards every label
  collected so far.
* Current Claude models think briefly before answering, so we ask for
  low `effort` and allow `max_tokens = 1024`. The reply can then contain
  a thinking block before the text, so we pick the block whose `type` is
  `"text"`; a `stop_reason` of `"refusal"` (the model declined) is
  recorded as a missing label.
* `parse_label_response()` digs the JSON out of the reply — models
  sometimes wrap it in prose or code fences, and sometimes invent labels
  outside the codebook — and maps anything unusable to `NA` with an
  error message.

The model is one constant, `DEFAULT_MODEL`, the current small Claude
model. Record the exact model string with your results; it is part of
your instrument. Models are listed at
<https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/models/overview>.

```{r annotator, eval=TRUE}
DEFAULT_MODEL <- "claude-haiku-5-5"

parse_label_response <- function(raw) {
  json <- str_extract(raw, "\\{[^}]*\\}")
  parsed <- if (is.na(json)) NULL else tryCatch(fromJSON(json), error = function(e) NULL)
  if (is.null(parsed)) {
    return(tibble(label = NA_character_, confidence = NA_real_, error = "invalid JSON"))
  }
  label <- parsed$label
  if (is.null(label) || !label %in% LABELS) {
    return(tibble(label = NA_character_, confidence = NA_real_,
                  error = paste0("invalid label: ", label %||% "(none)")))
  }
  tibble(label = label, confidence = as.numeric(parsed$confidence %||% NA_real_),
         error = NA_character_)
}

annotate_one <- function(text, model) {
  resp <- httr2::request("https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages") |>
    httr2::req_headers(
      "x-api-key" = Sys.getenv("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"),
      "anthropic-version" = "2023-06-01"
    ) |>
    httr2::req_body_json(list(
      model = model,
      max_tokens = 1024,
      output_config = list(effort = "low"),
      messages = list(list(role = "user", content = build_prompt(CODEBOOK, text)))
    )) |>
    httr2::req_retry(max_tries = 4) |>
    httr2::req_perform() |>
    httr2::resp_body_json()
  if (identical(resp$stop_reason, "refusal")) {
    return(tibble(label = NA_character_, confidence = NA_real_, error = "refused"))
  }
  text_block <- keep(resp$content, \(block) identical(block$type, "text"))
  parse_label_response(if (length(text_block)) text_block[[1]]$text else "")
}

annotate_posts_llm <- function(texts, model = DEFAULT_MODEL) {
  map(texts, \(text) {
    out <- tryCatch(
      annotate_one(text, model),
      error = function(e) tibble(label = NA_character_, confidence = NA_real_,
                                 error = paste("API error:", conditionMessage(e)))
    )
    Sys.sleep(0.5)   # be polite to the API's rate limits
    mutate(out, model = model)
  }) |> list_rbind()
}
```

The parser deserves a test on the failure modes you will actually see
in the wild — the same five cases the Python notebook tests:

```{r parser-tests, eval=TRUE}
test_responses <- c(
  '{"label": "politics", "confidence": 0.92}',            # clean JSON
  '```json\n{"label": "other", "confidence": 0.5}\n```',  # fenced
  'Sure! {"label": "science_tech", "confidence": 0.7}',   # prose-wrapped
  'This post is about politics.',                          # no JSON at all
  '{"label": "sports", "confidence": 1.0}'                 # not in the codebook
)
map(test_responses, parse_label_response) |>
  list_rbind() |>
  mutate(response = str_trunc(str_replace_all(test_responses, "\n", " "), 45),
         .before = 1)
```

Every case comes back as a clean label or an explicit `NA` with an
error message; nothing stops the loop. That is the property you want in
a job that runs thousands of times unattended: bad responses become
*rows you can count*, not crashes that lose the batch.

### 4.3 What will this cost?

Always run the back-of-envelope *before* the batch. `MODEL_PRICES`
records Anthropic's published prices for three model tiers, in dollars
per million tokens. Prices change: verify them at
<https://claude.com/pricing> before budgeting a real project. The
estimate uses the crude ~4-characters-per-token heuristic for the
codebook, the prompt scaffolding, and each post, plus an allowance per
post for the short JSON answer and the model's brief thinking (billed as
output) — the same arithmetic as the Python notebook's
`estimate_annotation_cost()`:

```{r cost, eval=TRUE}
# Published prices, US dollars per million tokens, as of October 2026.
# Verify at https://claude.com/pricing before use. (Haiku's price is
# for prompts under 100K tokens, which every annotation prompt here is.)
MODEL_PRICES <- tribble(
  ~model,              ~input_usd_per_mtok, ~output_usd_per_mtok,
  "claude-haiku-5-5",                 0.10,                 0.50,
  "claude-sonnet-5-5",                2.00,                10.00,
  "claude-opus-5-5",                  4.00,                20.00
)

estimate_annotation_cost <- function(texts, prices = MODEL_PRICES,
                                     output_tokens_per_post = 150) {
  overhead_tokens <- (nchar(CODEBOOK) + 600) / 4   # codebook + prompt scaffolding
  input_tokens <- sum(overhead_tokens + nchar(texts) / 4)
  output_tokens <- output_tokens_per_post * length(texts)
  prices |>
    mutate(n_posts = length(texts),
           est_input_tokens = floor(input_tokens),
           est_output_tokens = output_tokens,
           est_cost_usd = (input_tokens * input_usd_per_mtok +
                             output_tokens * output_usd_per_mtok) / 1e6,
           est_cost_per_1k_posts_usd = est_cost_usd / n_posts * 1000)
}

cost_table <- estimate_annotation_cost(gold$text)
cost_table
```

Read the per-1,000-posts column: even the largest tier costs a few
dollars per thousand posts, and the smallest costs pennies. Compare that
to crowd-worker rates of roughly \$0.05–0.15 *per label* — \$50–150 per
thousand posts before quality control — and you see why Gilardi et al.
(2023) reported a large cost advantage for LLM annotation. The tiers
also differ a great deal from one another, which is one more reason to
validate the cheap model before assuming you need the expensive one.
The bottleneck moves from labeling to validating.

### 4.4 Running the annotator (guarded)

Calls leave your machine and cost money, so the chunk runs only when an
API key is present, and otherwise explains what it would have done:

```{r run-llm, eval=TRUE}
if (nzchar(Sys.getenv("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"))) {
  llm_labels <- annotate_posts_llm(gold$text)
  gold$llm_label <- llm_labels$label
  dir.create("data", showWarnings = FALSE)
  write_csv(bind_cols(select(gold, uri, text), llm_labels), "data/llm_labels.csv")
  cat("Saved", nrow(llm_labels), "LLM labels to data/llm_labels.csv\n")
} else {
  est <- filter(cost_table, model == DEFAULT_MODEL)
  cat("No ANTHROPIC_API_KEY set, so no posts were sent to the API.\n",
      "It would send each gold post to ", DEFAULT_MODEL,
      " with the codebook prompt, sleep 0.5s between requests,\n",
      "parse the JSON labels, and cost about $",
      format(round(est$est_cost_usd, 2), nsmall = 2), ".\n", sep = "")
}
```

## 5. A baseline annotator that always runs

Never evaluate an exciting method without a boring one. The keyword
baseline is deliberately simple, fully transparent (you can read the
whole "model" in a minute), and perfectly reproducible. Its rules come
from the shared codebook file, and it applies them exactly as the Python
notebook does:

* lowercase the post;
* count whole-word matches of every keyword — `\b` in a regular
  expression marks a word boundary, so `ai` matches "AI" but not the
  "ai" inside "said", and `str_escape()` makes a keyword like `a.i` match
  a literal period;
* the category with the most matches wins, and a tie or no matches at
  all gives `other`.

> **A caution about our keyword lists.** They were written for news
> text by people who had already read the gold posts. That is "training
> on the test set" (Exercise 3 below), so the baseline's agreement with
> the gold labels is probably *optimistic*.

```{r baseline, eval=TRUE}
keyword_hits <- function(text) {
  lowered <- str_to_lower(text)
  map(KEYWORD_RULES, \(words) {
    counts <- map_int(words, \(w) str_count(lowered, regex(paste0("\\b", str_escape(w), "\\b"))))
    rep(words, counts)
  })
}

keyword_label <- function(text) {
  scores <- lengths(keyword_hits(text))
  best <- max(scores)
  if (best == 0 || sum(scores == best) > 1) DEFAULT_LABEL else names(scores)[scores == best]
}

map(KEYWORD_RULES, length)

examples <- c("The Senate passed the spending bill on Tuesday.",
              "Researchers published a new study of sleep and memory.",
              "Here is our best five-ingredient lasagna recipe.",
              "The tech company's president spoke at the conference.")
tibble(text = examples, label = map_chr(examples, keyword_label))
```

The last example is a **tie** — `president` for politics, `tech` for
science_tech — so it falls through to `other`. A tie-breaking rule is
part of the instrument just as much as the keyword lists are.

Now label all 60 gold posts and save the predictions next to the gold
labels, so the validation can be re-run from the file alone:

```{r baseline-gold, eval=TRUE}
gold <- gold |>
  mutate(baseline_label = map_chr(text, keyword_label))

dir.create("data", showWarnings = FALSE)
write_csv(select(gold, uri, text, gold_label, baseline_label),
          "data/baseline_predictions.csv")
count(gold, baseline_label)
```

## 6. Validation: how good is the automated annotator?

### 6.1 Accuracy, percent agreement, and Cohen's kappa

**Accuracy** (percent agreement) is the share of posts where machine and
human agree. **Cohen's kappa** corrects it for chance:
$\kappa = (p_o - p_e) / (1 - p_e)$, where $p_o$ is observed agreement and
$p_e$ is the agreement two coders would reach by guessing independently
with their own label frequencies. A coder that labels *everything* with
the most common category agrees with the gold standard often while
contributing no information — kappa exposes that, and the "lazy modal
coder" below shows it. The validation uses the LLM's labels when they
exist and the baseline's otherwise:

```{r metrics, eval=TRUE}
cohen_kappa <- function(truth, pred, labels) {
  cm <- table(factor(truth, levels = labels), factor(pred, levels = labels))
  n <- sum(cm)
  po <- sum(diag(cm)) / n
  pe <- sum(rowSums(cm) * colSums(cm)) / n^2
  (po - pe) / (1 - pe)
}

landis_koch <- function(k) {
  cut(k, breaks = c(-Inf, 0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8, 1),
      labels = c("poor", "slight", "fair", "moderate", "substantial", "almost perfect"))
}

annotator <- if ("llm_label" %in% names(gold)) "llm_label" else "baseline_label"
pred <- gold[[annotator]]

modal_label <- names(which.max(table(gold$gold_label)))
lazy <- rep(modal_label, nrow(gold))

tibble(
  annotator = c(annotator, paste0("always '", modal_label, "'")),
  accuracy = c(mean(gold$gold_label == pred), mean(gold$gold_label == lazy)),
  kappa = c(cohen_kappa(gold$gold_label, pred, LABELS),
            cohen_kappa(gold$gold_label, lazy, LABELS))
) |>
  mutate(landis_koch = landis_koch(kappa))
```

The lazy coder earns a respectable-looking accuracy from prevalence
alone, and a kappa of exactly 0: that is the **prevalence problem**, and
it is why you always report a chance-corrected statistic. Landis & Koch
(1977) offered conventional labels for kappa — 0.41–0.60 *moderate*,
0.61–0.80 *substantial*, 0.81 and above *almost perfect* — printed in
the last column. They are a convention, not a law: report the number,
publish the confusion matrix, and read the errors.

### Does R agree with Python?

Both implementations read the same codebook file and the same gold
labels and apply the same matching and tie rules, so R's baseline
labels should equal the Python notebook's saved predictions *post by
post*, and the metrics should match its saved metrics. This chunk checks
both, and stops the document if they differ:

```{r parity, eval=TRUE}
py_dir <- file.path("..", "..", "Notebooks", "Part 08 - LLMs as Research Assistants", "data")
python_predictions <- read_csv(file.path(py_dir, "baseline_predictions.csv"),
                               show_col_types = FALSE)
python_metrics <- read_csv(file.path(py_dir, "agreement_metrics.csv"),
                           show_col_types = FALSE)

python_value <- function(name) python_metrics$value[python_metrics$metric == name]

parity <- tibble(
  metric = c("accuracy", "cohen_kappa"),
  r = c(mean(gold$gold_label == gold$baseline_label),
        cohen_kappa(gold$gold_label, gold$baseline_label, LABELS)),
  python = c(python_value("accuracy"), python_value("cohen_kappa"))
) |>
  mutate(difference = round(r, 4) - python)
parity

same_labels <- identical(gold$baseline_label,
                         python_predictions$baseline_label[match(gold$uri, python_predictions$uri)])
cat("R and Python baseline labels identical on every post:", same_labels, "\n")
stopifnot("R and Python baseline labels differ" = same_labels,
          "R and Python agreement metrics differ" = all(abs(parity$difference) < 1e-9))
```

### 6.2 Confusion matrix

A confusion matrix cross-tabulates gold labels (rows) against machine
labels (columns): the diagonal is agreement, and each off-diagonal cell
is a specific, named kind of mistake. The heat map draws the same table,
with darker tiles for larger counts:

```{r confusion, eval=TRUE, fig.width=5.5, fig.height=4.5}
confusion <- table(gold = factor(gold$gold_label, LABELS),
                   machine = factor(pred, LABELS))
confusion

as_tibble(confusion) |>
  mutate(gold = factor(gold, rev(LABELS)), machine = factor(machine, LABELS)) |>
  ggplot(aes(machine, gold, fill = n)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = n, color = n > max(n) / 2), show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "white", `FALSE` = "black")) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#f0f4fa", high = "#08306b") +
  labs(x = "Machine label", y = "Gold (human) label", fill = "Posts",
       title = "Confusion matrix: annotator vs. gold labels") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Read the matrix by column first. Most errors sit in the `other` column:
posts the keyword lists failed to catch, which fall through to the
default label because their topic is carried by context rather than
vocabulary. The fewer errors in the `politics` column run the other
way: a political keyword in a story the codebook says is about
something else.

### 6.3 Per-category precision and recall

Overall numbers hide category-level failures, so compute, per category,
**precision** (when the machine says "politics," how often is it
right?), **recall** (of the truly political posts, how many did it
find?), and their harmonic mean, **F1**:

```{r per-class, eval=TRUE}
per_class <- map(LABELS, \(label) {
  tp <- sum(gold$gold_label == label & pred == label)
  fp <- sum(gold$gold_label != label & pred == label)
  fn <- sum(gold$gold_label == label & pred != label)
  precision <- if (tp + fp > 0) tp / (tp + fp) else 0
  recall <- if (tp + fn > 0) tp / (tp + fn) else 0
  tibble(category = label, precision, recall,
         f1 = if (precision + recall > 0) 2 * precision * recall / (precision + recall) else 0,
         support = tp + fn)
}) |> list_rbind()

per_class

per_class |>
  mutate(annotator = paste0(annotator, " (", CODEBOOK_VERSION, ")"),
         validated_at = format(today())) |>
  write_csv("data/agreement_metrics.csv")
```

For `science_tech`, precision is high but recall is much lower: the
baseline is right when it says science_tech, but it finds only some of
those posts, and with so few in the sample each miss costs a lot.
`other` absorbs every miss as the default label. An analysis of "the
science_tech posts" built on these labels would be clean but
*incomplete* — and not randomly incomplete, because it would
systematically miss technology stories told without technical
vocabulary. That is **measurement bias**, not just noise.

## 7. Error analysis: read the disagreements

Aggregate metrics tell you *how much* the annotator errs; only reading
the disagreements tells you *how*. For each disagreement we ask the
baseline to show its work — which keywords matched — and sort the
failures into three types:

```{r disagreements, eval=TRUE}
failure_type <- function(text) {
  counts <- lengths(keyword_hits(text))
  if (sum(counts) == 0) "no keywords matched"
  else if (n_distinct(counts) == 1) "tie between categories"
  else "a keyword from another category won"
}

disagreements <- gold |>
  filter(gold_label != baseline_label) |>
  mutate(
    matched = map_chr(text, \(t) {
      hits <- keep(keyword_hits(t), \(w) length(w) > 0)
      if (length(hits) == 0) "" else
        paste(imap_chr(hits, \(w, cat) paste0(cat, ": ", paste(w, collapse = ", "))),
              collapse = "; ")
    }),
    failure_type = map_chr(text, failure_type)
  )

disagreements |>
  transmute(text = str_trunc(text, 80), gold_label, baseline_label, matched, failure_type)

count(disagreements, failure_type, sort = TRUE)
```

Each failure type teaches something different:

* **No keywords matched.** The topic is carried entirely by context. A
  referee "denied permission to enter the U.S." is an immigration story
  to any human reader (rule 2), but no word on the politics list
  appears. These are exactly the errors an LLM with world knowledge
  should fix, and where you should concentrate your validation effort.
* **A keyword from another category won.** The vocabulary belongs to the
  setting rather than the subject: a mayor in a sports-business spat, a
  country's name in a story about World Cup tickets. Rules 2 and 3 exist
  for these cases, and a keyword counter can't apply them.
* **A tie between categories.** One keyword from each list, so the post
  falls through to `other`, hiding the fact that the baseline found
  *some* evidence for two topics.

None of these errors are random; each is predictable from the post's
wording, so a downstream analysis would inherit them systematically.
Error analysis also occasionally flags gold-label mistakes — human
coders err too, and validation cuts both ways.

## 8. When are LLM labels defensible as research measures?

Suppose you now add an API key, run Section 4.4, and find the LLM agrees
with your gold labels at kappa = 0.85. What does defensible use of those
labels look like? The emerging methodological consensus:

**Defensible practice**

* **Validate on a gold sample, every time.** Performance varies sharply
  across tasks, languages, and even prompt phrasings (Ziems et al.
  2024). A kappa from someone else's paper — or from your own *previous*
  project — does not transfer.
* **Version everything**: the exact codebook text, the exact prompt
  template, the exact model string (the value of `DEFAULT_MODEL`, not
  just "Claude"), the parameters, and the dates. The prompt + model
  **is** your instrument; readers must be able to inspect it, and you
  must be able to detect when it changes underneath you.
* **Report uncertainty.** Publish the confusion matrix and per-category
  precision and recall, not a single accuracy number. If you collected
  confidence scores, use them — route low-confidence posts to human
  review, or carry label uncertainty into downstream estimates rather
  than pretending the labels are exact.
* **Re-validate when anything changes** — a new time period, a new
  community, a new model version. Domain drift quietly degrades
  annotators that validated beautifully last year.

**Standing concerns**

* **Closed-model reproducibility.** Hosted models are updated and
  eventually retired; the same prompt can return different labels next
  year, and no parameter setting ever guaranteed identical outputs
  (Ollion et al. 2024). Mitigations: save every raw model response (not
  just the parsed labels), pin dated model versions where the provider
  offers them, and report collection dates — while recognizing that,
  unlike a keyword dictionary, a hosted instrument can never be
  perfectly frozen. Open-weight models trade some capability for
  genuine freezability.
* **Zero-shot vs. few-shot.** Our prompt is *zero-shot*: codebook, post,
  no worked examples. Adding a handful of labeled examples to the prompt
  (*few-shot*) often helps — Gilardi et al. (2023) found zero-shot
  ChatGPT already competitive with crowd workers, and Törnberg (2023)
  found it competitive with experts on political tweets, while Ziems et
  al. document task-dependent gains from examples. Few-shot examples are
  part of the instrument too: choose them deliberately (cover the edge
  cases, not just the easy wins), document them, and never let your
  validation posts leak into the prompt.
* **The benchmark perspective.** Ziems et al.'s multi-task benchmark is
  a useful prior: LLMs do best on tasks with crisp, surface-visible
  definitions (topic, relevance) and worst on subtle latent constructs
  (implicit stance, figurative language, expert framing tasks).
  Calibrate your expectations — and your validation-sample size — to
  where your task sits on that spectrum.
* **Bias auditing.** LLM errors are not random: models can be
  systematically better at labeling some dialects, communities, or
  viewpoints than others. If your research design compares groups,
  validate *within* each group, not just overall.

## Ethics and limitations

**Sending user content to third-party servers.** Every post you annotate
with a hosted LLM is transmitted to another company's infrastructure —
in our case Anthropic's. The posts here are public, but public
availability is not blanket consent (Fiesler & Proferes 2018), and users
who tolerated their posts being *read* may not expect them to be
*processed by an AI company*. Before annotating at scale: check the
provider's data-use and retention terms (whether API inputs are used for
training, and how long they are retained); minimize what you send — our
prompt contains only the post text, not handles, DIDs, or profile data;
consider your IRB's view on transmitting user data to a third party; and
prefer locally run open-weight models for sensitive populations or
topics where the transmission itself is the harm.

**One institutional account.** We deliberately annotated a news
organization's account: posts written for publication by an
institution, not a person's private expression. Topic-labeling an
arbitrary stranger's posting history produces a behavioral profile of a
person who never opted into being profiled. Legitimate designs exist
(public officials, aggregates across many accounts), but they need
justification — especially for categories more sensitive than "politics
vs. other."

**The gold standard is the weakest link here.** Sixty posts coded by the
tutorial authors, who also wrote the keyword lists, is a demonstration,
not a measurement. Real projects need multiple independent coders,
reported inter-coder reliability, and a validation sample sized to put
acceptably tight confidence intervals on kappa — 60 posts leaves wide
ones.

**Labels are not ground truth.** Even a perfect annotator only
reproduces the codebook's worldview. Our rule 2, for instance,
*constructs* a particular boundary between politics and sports rather
than discovering one. Automated content analysis scales your codebook's
assumptions right along with its categories (Grimmer & Stewart 2013).

**Representativeness.** One news organization's feed says nothing about
Bluesky at large — its posts are edited, headline-style text, unlike
most users' posts — and Bluesky's early-adopter, Twitter-migrant skew
says nothing about the general public (Mislove et al. 2011). The
pipeline transfers; the prevalence estimates do not.

## Exercises

1. **Extend the codebook to four categories.** Split `other` into
   `sports` and `lifestyle` (recipes, shopping advice, games, and the
   like), both common in `data/posts.csv`. Copy the shared
   `codebook.json` (its path is `CODEBOOK_PATH`), update `labels`, the
   codebook text, and the decision rules in your copy, then re-read 20
   posts and check that *you* can apply the new scheme consistently
   before asking any machine to. Notice how every added category creates
   new boundary disputes that need decision rules: is a story about a
   stadium's security budget `sports` or `politics`?
2. **Grow the gold standard and recompute.** Sample 20 posts from
   `data/posts.csv` that are *not* already in the gold file, hand-code
   them with the codebook, append them to a copy of the gold labels
   (leave the original 60 rows untouched), and re-run Sections 5–6. Does
   kappa move? With n = 80 instead of 60, your estimates also get more
   stable — small validation samples leave wide uncertainty around kappa.
3. **Be a second coder.** Have a classmate independently code 20 of the
   gold posts using *only* the codebook text (no peeking at
   `gold_label`), then compute the human–human Cohen's kappa with
   `cohen_kappa()`. Compare it to the machine–human kappa: agreement
   ceilings are properties of tasks, and the human–human number tells
   you what ceiling to expect.
4. **Improve the keyword baseline — carefully.** Read all of the
   disagreements from Section 7, add or remove keywords in
   `keyword_rules` in a copy of `codebook.json`, and re-run the
   validation. Then reflect: every fix you made used the gold sample
   itself, so your improved kappa is optimistic — you have effectively
   trained on your test set (as, the Section 5 caution admits, did the
   authors of the original lists). How would you measure the improvement
   honestly?
5. **Run the real LLM annotator and compare.** Get an API key from
   [Anthropic](https://docs.claude.com), set it with
   `Sys.setenv(ANTHROPIC_API_KEY = "...")` (or in `.Renviron`), and
   re-run Section 4.4 (cost: well under a dollar). Then re-run Sections
   6–7 with `gold$llm_label` in place of `baseline_label`. Where does the
   LLM beat the keywords — does it recover the "no keywords matched"
   posts from the error analysis? Where does it still disagree with the
   gold labels?
6. **Test prompt variations.** With a key, try at least two variants:
   (a) delete the DECISION RULES block from the codebook text before
   building prompts, and (b) add three labeled few-shot examples to the
   prompt (chosen from posts *outside* the gold sample — never let
   validation posts leak into the prompt). Recompute kappa for each
   variant. How sensitive is your "instrument" to its wording?

## Research project ideas

**1. Does one validation generalize across communities?** LLM
annotators are usually validated once, on one sample — but Bluesky hosts
very different communities. *Question:* does an annotator (LLM or
otherwise) validated on one community's posts perform equally well on
another's? *Data:* posts from accounts in two contrasting starter packs
or feeds (Part 09 shows how to enumerate them) — say, academic Bluesky
versus sports or fandom Bluesky. *Method:* one shared codebook; a
separate human-coded gold sample of 60–100 posts per community;
per-community kappa, confusion matrices, and error analyses; a
comparison of *where* the annotator fails in each. *Expected challenge:*
building genuinely comparable gold standards — the codebook will fit one
community better than the other, and you must disentangle annotator
failure from codebook misfit, which is itself a finding worth reporting.

**2. Prompt and model sensitivity as a measurement-stability study.** If
the prompt-plus-model is the instrument, how stable is the instrument?
*Question:* how much do labels change across reasonable paraphrases of
the same codebook, across zero-shot versus few-shot prompts, and across
model tiers (e.g., the Haiku, Sonnet, and Opus tiers listed in
`MODEL_PRICES`)? *Data:* a fixed corpus of ~500 posts plus a 100-post
gold sample. *Method:* a factorial grid of prompt variants × models; for
each cell, kappa against gold *and* pairwise label-flip rates between
cells; identify which posts flip under every perturbation. *Expected
challenge:* cost grows with the grid, and you must separate instrument
instability from genuine ambiguity — posts that flip across prompts are
often posts human coders would also dispute, so collect human
disagreement data on the flippers.

**3. Validated prevalence estimation for political talk on Bluesky.**
Much published Twitter work estimated the *prevalence* of some content
category (incivility, misinformation engagement, political talk).
*Question:* what share of posting by a defined population on Bluesky —
e.g., accounts in a journalism starter pack — is political, and how did
it change around a major news event (Part 05's event-study skills)?
*Data:* author feeds for 50–100 accounts over several months. *Method:*
LLM annotation at scale, validated against a stratified gold sample;
crucially, correct the headline prevalence estimate for classifier error
rather than just counting predicted labels, in the spirit of Hopkins &
King (2010), since even a high-kappa annotator with asymmetric errors
(like our baseline's low `science_tech` recall) biases raw category
proportions. *Expected challenge:* misclassification correction needs
good estimates of the error rates themselves, which pushes you toward a
larger gold sample — budget your human-coding time as seriously as your
API spend.
